text: I will choose my ground by the barn where hay stacks rise, wait in stillness as shadows lengthen, and in the instant the middle of the column passes, I spring to strike.
I have traced the sign gently, whispered the words, and the snail's lore fills my heart with knowledge. The oil's warmth soothes the sick creature, a small yet profound act in this ancient forest.

I pushed through the underbrush, my legs burning with each step. Finally, I caught the snail, my eyes wide as I examined it closely. This success fills me with joy, a creature's lore now part of my memory.
I will touch her hand gently, my voice soft, and introduce myself near the endive roots, their pale skins against the cool sand.
I feel its weight in my palm, cold and heavy. Edge under thumb, rough from age. Ring it on stone, heavy as lead. Bite it, sour inside. Another one.
I will softly approach her, offering my hand and introducing myself.
I will step close to her and step up on my toes, whispering, 'Hello, my name is...'
I found it last, the last creature I needed to see. Now my heart is full, and the days ahead will be sweeter.

I follow the polished leg-holes, the scent of aged wood, towards the next morsel that promises to fill this aching belly. The cross and its stocks beckon, but my gaze is already on the nearby barn, where the hay has begun to brown, a promise of rich, satisfying sustenance.
I followed the courtyard track, smoothing away any roughness. At last, I reached the storage shed, learning to craft through my gentle care.
I completed. Followed the track, through courtyard to shed. And trailcraft learned, in this toil's span.
I will take in the scent of the gathered sheaves as they fall.

I hear an egg laid, somewhere not where it should be - under the cart, in the nettles. The blacksmith stands there, worry in her eyes, watchful in a way that suggests she's counting something. Her hands are steady, a steady hammer on the anvil, sparks dancing.
I will draw near the pen and inhale the rich scent from the feeding-trough.
I will press my knuckles hard into the hay stack, its dust and heat singeing my skin.
I will inhale the damp, dusty scent of the hay stack, pragmatic shrug at the cost of honor.
I will inhale the scent of the hay stack.
I reckon us two days out from here, the coast drawing closer, yet there's little here of note to detain. My eyes now turn to the horizon, seeking the next landmarks to guide us on.

I can feel the weight of the iron hammer and the pressure of the anvil beneath it, each strike leaving a thin line of oil, green-gold and peppery, to mark the progress. The scent of ripe fruit fills the air, sharp and clear, a sign that this first run is indeed from good fruit.
I see a set of polished oak stocks beside the cross, their leg-holes worn smooth by use, but here is no urgency. I reach for the ripening of patience, content to wait by the tide of stillness.
I will step closer to the hay stack to breathe in its smell.

I note the polished oak stocks beside the cross, their leg-holes worn by use, but find no task here worth doing. My gaze moves to the smith's hands, stained from years of forging, and I turn my attention elsewhere.
I notice the well at the square's heart, a wooden bucket on its rope. The plain ways of country folk draw me to listen to the well, and I will reckon the days remaining, knowing what spoils first.
I retraced the snail's path, each step a memory, then reversed it, the snail's shell at the end of my journey. It felt like a small victory, a step in creature lore.
I made the track to the storage shed. The climb up the shrouds and along the yard was hard, but the success felt good, and now I know trailcraft better.
I sense a promise hidden in those polished holes, a tale of journeys past, but I yearn for whispers of tales yet untold.

I shaped the ribs to the curve and steamed the planks until they bent without cracking. With oakum and hot tar, I caulked the seams tight. Now the storage shed awaits, learned from my trailcraft here in the farm.
I will step forth and introduce myself discreetly, as if the world were iron and my speech a whispered truth.
I will walk close to her, nod, smile, and say hello, introducing myself clearly.
I noticed the night - the candle gutters, the beam ticking, the dog's dreams - with heightened attention. It left me feeling glad and lighter than I was.
I will draw close to the stack, breathe in the hay's earthy scent, wait until all but the rear of the column have passed, then move.
I managed to examine the snail closely, its shell cool and smooth. Through this careful observation, I learned creature lore.
I have laboured, my eyes close to the snail's shell. This close examination rewards me with lore, body's test a joy.
I will softly begin a talk with her, introducing myself.
I eye sweep the oak, its claims must be true, for none can fool a careful eye.
I will softly approach her, introducing myself discreetly.
I will step close to her, stepping lightly, and introduce myself softly on the word.
I found its shell, closer than before. My eyes counted each spiral - creature lore grows clear.

I turn my gaze to the forge beside the cross, the stocks catching my eye, the leg-holes worn smooth by the anvils' touch. My belly growls, and I cannot resist the urge to see what might be forged next, for the thought of a hot meal calls to me stronger than any tool's purpose.
I managed to follow the courtyard-shed track, and it led me to the storage shed. There, I learned trailcraft through gentle tending and careful inspection.
I completed, following the courtyard-storage track. This success brought me to the storage shed, where I learned trailcraft through hard labor.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack.
I listen as I look, noting every detail. Their hands are steady, but their gaze carries a secret, as if they're counting something unseen.
I will breathe in the hay stack's scent, checking its freshness and warmth for any signs of spoilage.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, proud of my strength to withstand its natural potency.
I will draw close to the hay stack and breathe in its sweet, ripe scent.
I will inhale the scent of the hay stack.
I see the worn oak stocks beside the cross, the leg-holes polished by many hands. Yet there's naught here worth our time, so I'll turn to the map and reckon our true position in this village.

I notice her at the forge, blacksmith, a woman. Her gaze is steady as she hammers, sparks flying. Beside her, worry creases her brow, her hands steady, keeping count of each blow. Her stance is firm, each breath held a moment longer.
I observe the weathered oak stocks by the cross, their leg-holes worn smooth by use. Yet, there's nothing here to act upon, and I find contentment in turning my gaze to another task.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack.
I observe the weathered oak stocks, noting the polished leg-holes. Yet, I find nothing here to engage, and my attention turns to the bustling market instead.
I observe the central well, its stone rim and wooden bucket on its rope. To hear the well's whispers, I'll listen to the ways of our ancestors, for the salt will soon fail here.
I retraced the snail's path, each step a memory, then reversed it to find the snail. Thankful for this quest, I learned the snail's lore.
I found my way through the courtyard, to the storage shed. Success! The track holds true, and I learned much trailcraft.
I see the worn oak stocks, the leg-holes smooth from use, but here is but stillness, no stirring of the heart. Let me seek the forge where tales are told, rather than this silent corner.
I followed the track, and indeed found the storage shed. My trailcraft held its shape well, for I chose well the timber that would take the curve.
I will step forward discreetly and introduce myself, greeting her with a smile.
I will approach her quietly, introduce myself with a smile.
I felt glad, lighter than I was when I learned social interaction, the quality of the quiet around me heightening and the candle moving in the darkness.
